g11-biology-ub3-t1.overview: Enzymes are biological catalysts — proteins (and some RNAs) that speed reactions by lowering activation energy without being consumed. This topic establishes what enzymes are, why life needs them, and the naming/classification conventions.
objectives: Define catalyst and biological catalyst
Explain why uncatalyzed reactions are too slow for life
State the chemical nature of enzymes (protein, ribozyme exceptions)
Use the -ase naming convention and substrate-reaction pattern
List the six IUBMB enzyme classes with one example each
g11-biology-ub3-t1.simple: A catalyst speeds a chemical reaction and emerges unchanged. Enzymes are life's catalysts — almost all proteins (a few RNAs, ribozymes, also catalyze). Why does life need them? Because the reactions that keep you alive — breaking down glucose, copying DNA, building proteins — are far too slow on their own at body temperature: hydrogen peroxide in your cells would take ~300 years to decompose at the rate it does without catalase, which handles millions of molecules per second. Enzymes achieve this by lowering activation energy — the energy hill reactants must climb to react — without changing the reaction's start and end points (they speed forward AND reverse equally, and never make impossible reactions happen). Naming: the substrate + the reaction + the suffix -ase: lactase breaks lactose; DNA polymerase builds DNA; lipase breaks lipids. The six official classes by reaction type: oxidoreductases (electron transfers — dehydrogenases), transferases (move groups — kinases move phosphate), hydrolases (water-splitting digestion — protease, amylase, lipase), lyases (cut without water, often forming double bonds — decarboxylases), isomerases (rearrange — mutases), ligases (join two molecules with ATP — synthetases, DNA ligase). Every cell runs thousands of these reactions simultaneously, each on its own enzyme's command — that's metabolism.
g11-biology-ub3-t1.detailed:
The catalysis problem. At 37 °C most biochemical reactions proceed at rates incompatible with life: peptide bond hydrolysis takes centuries uncatalyzed; orotidine decarboxylase accelerates it 10¹⁷-fold (one of the largest known rate enhancements — a billion years compressed to milliseconds). Rate depends on the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ activation energy (Ea); enzymes lower Ea by stabilizing the transition state — they bind the transition state more tightly than substrate or product, providing an alternative reaction path. Enzymes do NOT alter ΔG (free-energy change), equilibrium constants, or reaction direction — they only make equilibrium arrive faster (both directions equally — the same enzyme catalyzes synthesis and breakdown depending on conditions).

Chemical nature. Proteins: globular, with the active site a small 3D cleft (~<2% of residues) formed by residues brought together from distant parts of the sequence. Cofactors: many enzymes need non-protein helpers — metal ions (Mg²⁺ for kinases, Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase, Fe in catalase, Cu in oxidases) and coenzymes (organic carriers — NAD⁺/FAD carry electrons, CoA carries acyl groups, vitamins are coenzyme precursors: B vitamins' essentiality is largely coenzyme chemistry). Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor. Ribozymes: RNA with catalytic activity (the ribosome's peptidyl transferase is rRNA — the ribozyme proof; RNase P; self-splicing introns) — evidence for the RNA-world hypothesis.

Nomenclature. Common names (trypsin, pepsin) persist; systematic: substrate + reaction type + -ase (lactose galactohydrolase = lactase). EC numbers: four digits — class, subclass, sub-subclass, serial (EC 1.1.1.1 = alcohol dehydrogenase: oxidoreductase, acting on CH-OH, NAD⁺ acceptor, #1). The six classes: (1) oxidoreductases — dehydrogenases/oxidases/reductases (lactate dehydrogenase); (2) transferases — kinases (hexokinase transfers ATP phosphate to glucose), transaminases; (3) hydrolases — esterases, glycosidases, peptidases (sucrase, lipase, pepsin); (4) lyases — C–C/C–O bond cleavage without hydrolysis, often reversible additions (pyruvate decarboxylase, citrate synthase's reverse); (5) isomerases — racemases, mutases (phosphoglucomutase); (6) ligases — synthetases joining with ATP hydrolysis (DNA ligase, glutamine synthetase). The '-ase' suffix marks the enzyme; the root tells the job.

Historical arc. Pasteur (fermentation needs living yeast) vs Liebig (cell extract suffices) → Buchner's 1897 zymase extract proved cell-free fermentation — enzymes are molecules, not vital forces. Sumner crystallized urease (1926 — enzymes are proteins), Northrop pepsin; the ribozyme discovery (Altman & Cech, 1980s) broke the 'all enzymes are protein' rule. Enzymology made biochemistry quantitative — and made metabolism a map of named reactions.

workedExamples.problem: Uncatalyzed, a reaction takes 300 years; catalase does it in 1 ms. What did the enzyme change and what did it NOT change?
workedExamples.substitution: changed: activation energy (path via transition-state stabilization) → rate; NOT changed: ΔG, equilibrium position, the reaction's direction or feasibility
workedExamples.answer: Enzymes are kinetic agents, not thermodynamic ones — they change how fast, not how far

workedExamples.problem: Classify by EC class: (a) hexokinase, (b) catalase, (c) DNA ligase, (d) triose-phosphate isomerase.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) transfers phosphate from ATP → transferase; (b) decomposes H₂O₂ (electron dismutation) → oxidoreductase; (c) joins DNA with ATP → ligase; (d) rearranges within a molecule → isomerase
workedExamples.answer: Transferase, oxidoreductase, ligase, isomerase

workedExamples.problem: A recipe: 'amylase.' Decode the name into substrate, reaction and source logic.
workedExamples.substitution: amylum (starch) + -ase → starch-digesting hydrolase; salivary + pancreatic amylase cleave starch to maltose — the name predicts the job
workedExamples.answer: Amylase = the starch hydrolase — names encode function

workedExamples.problem: Why do B-vitamin deficiencies cause disease if vitamins contain no energy?
workedExamples.substitution: B vitamins are coenzyme precursors (B₁→TPP, B₂→FAD, B₃→NAD⁺, B₆→PLP) — without them, apoenzymes can't form active holoenzymes → specific metabolic blocks (B₁ lack → beriberi: pyruvate dehydrogenase stalls)
workedExamples.answer: Vitamins build coenzymes; deficiency removes enzyme function — energy pathways jam

workedExamples.problem: The ribosome catalyzes peptide-bond formation but is mostly RNA. What does this prove?
workedExamples.substitution: peptidyl transferase activity resides in rRNA (protein removed still catalyzes) → RNA can be an enzyme → supports the RNA-world hypothesis (RNA both stores information and catalyzes — the first self-replicator)
workedExamples.calculation: the central machine is a ribozyme
workedExamples.answer: Not all enzymes are protein — RNA catalysis is real and ancient

Thinking enzymes shift equilibrium — they accelerate both directions equally
'Enzymes are used up in digestion' — they catalyze and emerge unchanged (though proteins get digested themselves in the gut!)
Believing the active site is a linear slice of the sequence — it's a 3D cleft from folded distant residues

Assuming -ase always means digestive — polymerases, kinases, synthetases build too
applications: Brewing and injera fermentation: amylase and zymase chemistry — Buchner's cell-free lesson in every teff ferment
Lactase supplements: the -ase naming predicts the product's job (lactose hydrolysis)
Detergent enzymes: proteases/amylases/lipases digesting stains at 30 °C — industrial catalysis
Medicine: statins target HMG-CoA reductase; EC knowledge underpins drug design
Diagnosis: blood LDH/ALT/AST levels flag heart/liver damage — enzymes as biomarkers
g11-biology-ub3-t1.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts — mostly proteins, some RNAs — that accelerate life's reactions by lowering activation energy and stabilizing the transition state, without being consumed or altering equilibrium. They require cofactors (metals, coenzymes from vitamins) to form active holoenzymes. Named by substrate + reaction + -ase and sorted into six EC classes (oxidoreductase, transferase, hydrolase, lyase, isomerase, ligase), enzymes constitute the machinery of metabolism.

g11-biology-ub3-t2.overview: Enzyme properties and functions: specificity (one enzyme, one reaction type), extreme catalytic power, mild-condition operation, reversibility, and regulation — plus the central role enzymes play in metabolic pathways and cell function.
objectives: Explain enzyme specificity: absolute, group, linkage, stereochemical
Relate enzyme structure (active site) to its properties
Describe catalytic power quantitatively (turnover number)
Explain how enzymes function in metabolic pathways
Give examples of enzyme roles in digestion, DNA, muscle, detox
g11-biology-ub3-t2.simple: Five properties define enzymes. 1) Specificity: each enzyme recognizes one substrate or one reaction type — urease acts on urea and almost nothing else (absolute); proteases cleave peptide bonds generally (group/linkage specificity); and most distinguish L from D forms (stereo-specific — your body builds proteins from L-amino acids only). Specificity comes from the active site's 3D shape and chemical pattern — a lock-and-key fit refined into induced fit (the site hugs the substrate and adjusts). 2) Catalytic power: turnover numbers — catalase processes 40 million H₂O₂ molecules per second; each enzyme molecule works thousands of times per second. 3) Mild conditions: enzymes run at body temperature, neutral pH, normal pressure — unlike industrial chemistry's heat/pressure/acid (detergent enzymes and industrial amylases work where harsh chemicals would). 4) No consumption: unchanged after each cycle — tiny amounts catalyze large conversions. 5) Regulation: cells switch enzymes on/off (hormones, inhibitors, compartmentalization) — enzymes are controlled machinery, not free agents. Functionally, enzymes ARE metabolism: digestion (amylase → maltase; pepsin → peptidases; lipase + bile), DNA copying (polymerase, ligase, helicase), protein synthesis (the ribosome), muscle contraction (myosin ATPase), liver detox (cytochrome P450s), and the pathway logic — products of enzyme 1 feed enzyme 2 in sequence (glucose → 10 enzyme steps → pyruvate), so one missing enzyme blocks one step (and causes a disease — PKU: phenylalanine builds up without its hydroxylase).
g11-biology-ub3-t2.detailed:
Specificity types. Absolute: one substrate only (urease, glucokinase vs hexokinase's broader range). Group (bond-type): acts on a class — pepsin cleaves many peptides at hydrophobic residues; lipases on ester bonds. Linkage: α-amylase hits α-1,4 glycosidic bonds but not β-1,4 (cellulose passes through us undigested — the fiber explanation; ruminants solve it with microbial cellulase). Stereochemical: L-amino-acid oxidase ignores D-forms; our receptors, enzymes and DNA are all chiral-selective — the basis of drug enantiomer differences (thalidomide's lesson). Molecular origin: the active site's complementary shape + charge/H-bond pattern; induced fit (Koshland): substrate binding reshapes the site to grip the transition state — explains both specificity and catalysis.

Catalytic power metrics. Turnover number (kcat): substrate molecules per enzyme per second — catalase 4×10⁷, carbonic anhydrase 10⁶, hexokinase ~100 (slow but regulated). Specificity constant kcat/Km compares efficiency at low substrate — diffusion limit ~10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ (acetylcholinesterase and carbonic anhydrase approach it — 'perfect enzymes'). Rate enhancements vs uncatalyzed: 10⁶–10¹² typical. One enzyme molecule processes its own weight in substrate every few seconds.

Function in pathways. Metabolism = enzyme-organized reaction networks: catabolic (breakdown, energy harvest — glycolysis, Krebs, β-oxidation) and anabolic (synthesis — gluconeogenesis, fatty-acid synthesis, translation). Pathway logic: sequential steps with small free-energy changes (many small hills beat one huge cliff), branch points (metabolite pools feed alternatives), and regulation at committed steps (allosteric — see t5). Compartmentalization: lysosome (acid hydrolases — pH optimum ~5 matches the compartment, protecting the cytosol at pH 7.2), mitochondria (Krebs + ETC), chloroplast stroma/thylakoid (Calvin), cytosol (glycolysis) — location controls which reactions meet which enzymes. Enzyme levels themselves are controlled: gene expression (lactose induces β-galactosidase — the operon), degradation, zymogen activation (pepsinogen→pepsin by acid; trypsinogen→trypsin by enterokinase — digestive enzymes stored safely, fired on demand).

Physiological roles (survey). Digestion: the hydrolysis toolkit (carbohydrases, proteases, lipases, nucleases) — each with pH optimum matching its compartment (pepsin acid-stomach; trypsin alkaline-small intestine; salivary amylase neutral-mouth). DNA: replication (helicase unwinds, polymerase copies, ligase seals, topoisomase relieves), repair, transcription (RNA polymerase). Energy: ATP synthase (the rotary motor — 100+ rev/s), myosin ATPase (contraction), Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out/2 K⁺ in per ATP — the resting potential's pump, ~25% of our resting energy!). Defense: lysozyme (tears/saliva — bacterial wall hydrolase), complement cascade (protease cascade amplified), clotting (thrombin cascade). Detox: P450 oxidations, catalase/peroxidase on reactive oxygen species. The cell is an enzyme machine, and its properties — specificity, power, mildness, regulation — are the properties of life's chemistry.

workedExamples.problem: Humans digest starch (α-1,4) but not cellulose (β-1,4) though both are glucose polymers. Explain.
workedExamples.substitution: amylase's active site fits the α-linkage's bond geometry; β-1,4 presents a different angle/shape — no binding, no catalysis; ruminants/termites host microbes with cellulases
workedExamples.answer: Linkage specificity: enzymes read bond geometry, not just composition — fiber passes through

workedExamples.problem: Catalase kcat = 4×10⁷/s. How many H₂O₂ molecules can ONE catalase molecule destroy in a minute?
workedExamples.answer: One catalase handles billions of molecules per minute — catalytic power in numbers

workedExamples.problem: Pepsin works at pH 2, trypsin at pH 8. Explain the physiological design.
workedExamples.substitution: active-site ionizable groups need specific protonation states; each enzyme evolved for its compartment's pH — stomach acid (pepsinogen activated only there), duodenum (bicarbonate-neutralized; trypsin's optimum); mismatch = denaturation/inactivity
workedExamples.answer: Enzymes are tuned to where they work — the pH gradient of the gut is an enzyme-switching system

workedExamples.problem: Why are digestive proteases secreted as zymogens?
workedExamples.substitution: active proteases would digest the cells that make them (pancreas autodigestion = pancreatitis); inactive precursors activate only in the lumen (pepsinogen + HCl; trypsinogen + enterokinase) — activation is compartment-restricted
workedExamples.answer: Zymogens keep dangerous enzymes switched off until they reach the gut

workedExamples.problem: A genetic defect deletes one enzyme in a 10-step pathway. Predict the biochemical signature.
workedExamples.substitution: substrate of the missing step accumulates (toxic in PKU — phenylalanine → intellectual disability), downstream product is deficient (melatonin/tyrosine derivatives ↓ — the PKU 'fair skin/hair' clue); treatment: restrict the accumulating substrate (low-Phe diet)
workedExamples.calculation: one gene, one enzyme, one disease
workedExamples.answer: Accumulation before the block, deficiency after — the inborn-error-of-metabolism pattern

commonMistakes: 'Specificity = only one substrate ever' — specificity has grades (absolute → group → linkage → stereo)
Thinking enzymes work fastest at any pH — each has a narrow optimum set by active-site chemistry
Confusing turnover number with total reaction rate — kcat is per enzyme molecule
Believing the cell's enzymes all float together — compartmentalization assigns enzymes to addresses
Calling cellulose 'indigestible fiber = useless' — it feeds gut microbes and drives peristalsis
Assuming zymogens are 'dead' — they're precisely timed safety switches
Thinking one enzyme = one reaction forever — many catalyze the reverse (lactate dehydrogenase runs both ways by conditions)
applications: PKU newborn screening: the pathway-block signature (high Phe) detected by enzyme/metabolite assay
Lactose intolerance: lactase persistence/non-persistence — a human enzyme polymorphism in the diet
Drug design: ACE inhibitors, statins, protease inhibitors (HIV) — targeting enzyme active sites
Food industry: bromelain (pineapple tenderizer), rennet (chymosin) in cheese — enzyme specificity exploited
Forensics: DNA profiling depends on restriction enzymes' sequence specificity
g11-biology-ub3-t2.summary: Enzymes combine specificity (absolute, group, linkage, stereochemical — from active-site geometry and induced fit), catalytic power (turnover numbers to 10⁷/s), mild-condition operation, non-consumption, and regulation. They constitute metabolism: pathway sequences with committed steps, compartmentalized by organelles, deployed as zymogens when dangerous, and individually essential — one missing enzyme defines an inborn error. Life's chemistry is enzyme chemistry.

g11-biology-ub3-t3.overview: Protein structure at four levels — primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix/β-sheet by backbone H-bonds), tertiary (3D folding of side chains), quaternary (multi-subunit assembly) — and the structure→function logic that enzymes, antibodies and hemoglobin depend on.
objectives: Describe primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure
Identify the bonds stabilizing each level
Relate folding to the amino-acid sequence (Anfinsen's rule)
Explain denaturation and its consequences
Give fibrous vs globular protein examples
g11-biology-ub3-t3.simple: Proteins are chains of amino acids (20 kinds; general formula: central carbon + amino group + carboxyl group + variable R group) linked by peptide bonds. Their architecture has four levels. Primary: the amino-acid sequence itself, written N→C terminus — set by the gene; sickle-cell anemia is one letter wrong (glutamate → valine at position 6 of β-globin). Secondary: local folding patterns stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms — the α-helix (coiled spring; keratin, hair) and β-pleated sheet (side-by-side strands; silk fibroin, spider dragline), plus turns/loops. Tertiary: the full 3D shape of one chain, driven by side-chain (R-group) interactions — hydrophobic residues bury inside (the folding's main force), hydrophilic stay outside in water; plus disulfide bridges (cysteine–cysteine covalent bonds — the hair 'perm' chemistry), ionic salt bridges, H-bonds, van der Waals. Quaternary: multiple folded chains assembling into one machine — hemoglobin = 4 subunits (2α + 2β), DNA polymerase, the ribosome, collagen's triple helix. Shape = function: enzymes' active sites are folding products; antibodies grip antigens by shape; collagen's triple helix is tensile armor; keratin's coils are hair and horn. Fibrous proteins (collagen, keratin, elastin, fibrin) = structural, insoluble, repetitive; globular proteins (enzymes, hemoglobin, antibodies, insulin) = compact, soluble, functional machines. Folding assistance: chaperones prevent misfolding; misfolded proteins aggregate — prions (mad cow) and amyloid plaques (Alzheimer's) are proteins with the wrong shape that corrupt other proteins' shapes. Denaturation: heat/pH/detergents unravel tertiary structure → function lost (the cooked egg white never un-cooks); some proteins refold when conditions return (ribonuclease — Anfinsen's experiment: the sequence contains all the folding information).
g11-biology-ub3-t3.detailed:
Amino-acid chemistry. H₂N–CHR–COOH; the R group defines the type: nonpolar (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro — the helix-breaker, Phe, Met), polar uncharged (Ser, Thr, Cys — disulfide maker, Asn, Gln, Tyr), acidic (Asp, Glu — negative at pH 7), basic (Lys, Arg, His — positive; His buffers and sits in active sites). Zwitterion: amino acids carry both charges at neutral pH; peptide bond formation (condensation, ribosome-catalyzed) creates the backbone — planar, trans, partial double-bond character — with repeating –N–Cα–C– units; the R groups project for interaction.

Secondary structure. Backbone H-bonds: C=O···H–N every 4 residues → α-helix (3.6 residues/turn, right-handed; i→i+4 bonds; keratin coiled-coils, myosin); alternate H-bond pattern (i→i+2/3) → β-sheets (parallel/antiparallel; silk fibroin's alternating Gly-Ser; spider silk's strength+elasticity from sheet crystals in an amorphous matrix). Turns (β-turns: 4 residues, often Gly/Asn) and loops reverse direction and carry most functional surfaces. Ramachandran plots: allowed φ/ψ angles — Pro restricts, Gly is flexible.

Tertiary folding. The hydrophobic effect dominates: nonpolar side chains collapse inward (entropy of water drives it — the biggest single force); plus H-bonds (Ser/Thr/Tyr OH), salt bridges (Asp⁻···Lys⁺), disulfides (2 Cys → Cys–Cys covalent — extracellular proteins are cross-linked; insulin's 3 bridges), van der Waals packing (the interior is crystal-dense). Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment: denature with urea + β-mercaptoethanol, remove them → refolds spontaneously → the sequence specifies the native conformation. Chaperonins (Hsp60/GroEL: the folding cage; Hsp70: the clamp) assist in vivo — preventing aggregation in the crowded cytosol; not all proteins fold alone.

Quaternary & assemblies. Subunits (protomers) assemble via the same forces: hemoglobin α₂β₂ (cooperativity — see below), tubulin α/β dimers → microtubules, actin G→F, viral capsids (symmetric self-assembly), the ribosome (rRNA + dozens of proteins). Advantages: smaller genes to copy/fold, cooperative regulation (allosteric transitions across subunits), error-correction (swap a bad subunit), and symmetry-based assembly.

Fibrous vs globular; examples. Fibrous: collagen (Gly-X-Y repeats → triple helix; 1/3 of body protein; bone/skin/tendon — vitamin C needed for hydroxylation — scurvy = weak collagen), keratin (coiled-coil intermediate filaments — hair, nails, horn; disulfide density sets curl/perm), elastin (random-coil spring — lungs, arteries), fibrin (the clot mesh). Globular: myoglobin (O₂ store — the single-chain model of folding), hemoglobin (transport with cooperativity), immunoglobulins (Y-shaped; variable loops = antigen recognition), insulin (small hormone; 51 aa, 3 disulfides), albumin (osmotic + carrier). Prions: PrP^C (α-helix-rich, soluble) → PrP^Sc (β-sheet-rich, aggregates) — the misfolded shape templates the conversion (mad cow/CJD); amyloidoses (Alzheimer's Aβ, Parkinson's α-synuclein) share the cross-β aggregate logic. Sickle-cell: the β6 Glu→Val hydrophobic patch polymerizes deoxy-Hb into fibers — one amino acid, one disease, structure→function proven.

workedExamples.problem: Anfinsen denatured ribonuclease and it refolded spontaneously. What principle did this establish, and where does it fail?

workedExamples.problem: Spider silk is stronger than steel by weight yet stretches. Connect the structure to both properties.
workedExamples.substitution: antiparallel β-sheet nanocrystals (Gly-Ala blocks — H-bond ladders) provide tensile strength; amorphous Gly-Ser-rich helical regions provide elasticity; the two-phase fiber = strength + extensibility
workedExamples.answer: Alternating hard crystals and soft springs — nature's composite engineering

g11-biology-ub3-t3.summary: Proteins build in four levels: primary (gene-set amino-acid sequence), secondary (α-helix/β-sheet from backbone H-bonds), tertiary (side-chain-driven 3D fold — hydrophobic core, disulfides, salt bridges; sequence-determined per Anfinsen, chaperone-assisted in cells), and quaternary (multi-subunit machines like hemoglobin). Fibrous proteins are materials; globular proteins are machines. Shape is function: one substitution causes sickle-cell, one misfold class causes prion disease, and denaturation proves the structure-function bond.

g11-biology-ub3-t4.overview: Enzyme–substrate models: the lock-and-key (Fischer) vs induced-fit (Koshland) pictures, the enzyme–substrate complex, the transition-state stabilization that powers catalysis, and the energy diagrams that make it all visible.
objectives: State the lock-and-key model and its limitation
Explain induced fit and why it superseded lock-and-key
Describe the ES complex and the catalytic cycle
Interpret activation-energy diagrams with/without enzyme
List catalytic mechanisms: proximity, strain, acid-base, covalent
g11-biology-ub3-t4.simple: How does an enzyme grip its substrate? The old picture (1894, Fischer): lock and key — the active site is a rigid pre-shaped cavity that exactly matches the substrate. It explains specificity but not catalysis (a perfect fit to the substrate would actually stabilize it — the opposite of reacting!) and not how enzymes accelerate. The modern picture (1958, Koshland): induced fit — the site is complementary not to the substrate but to the transition state; substrate binding reshapes the enzyme (and the substrate) so catalytic groups align, water is squeezed out, and the substrate is strained toward its reaction geometry. The cycle: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P (the enzyme–substrate complex is the intermediate; then products form and release — the enzyme resets). On an energy diagram: the uncatalyzed reaction has a tall activation-energy hill; the enzyme provides a path whose peak (the ES* transition state) is lower — reactants and products sit at the same heights either way (ΔG unchanged). The catalytic toolkit inside the site: proximity and orientation (holding two substrates together in the right pose — a huge entropic win), bond strain (bending the substrate toward the transition state), acid–base catalysis (His/Asp/Glu donate/accept protons at pH 7 — impossible in plain water), covalent catalysis (a transient enzyme–substrate bond — chymotrypsin's acyl-enzyme), and microenvironment (a hydrophobic pocket changes pKa values so chemistry runs that water would forbid). The transition-state analog trick proves the model: drugs shaped like the transition state bind enzymes far tighter than substrates do (statins mimic the HMG-CoA reductase transition state).
g11-biology-ub3-t4.detailed:
Lock-and-key. Fischer's complementarity explained specificity beautifully — and fails on three counts: (1) enzymes are flexible, not rigid; (2) perfect ground-state complementarity would lower the ES energy and INCREASE Ea (thermodynamic pit — the enzyme would hold the substrate too tightly); (3) it doesn't explain catalysis itself. The model survives as a specificity metaphor only.

Induced fit & conformational selection. Koshland: substrate binding induces active-site closure/realignment — hexokinase clamps around glucose (excluding water so ATP isn't wasted on it); glucokinase's open/closed states; the 'clasping hands' of HIV protease. Modern refinement: conformational selection — the enzyme samples conformations in solution; the substrate binds and traps the catalytically competent one. Both agree: the productive complex is assembled by binding, and the site is complementary to the transition state (Pauling's 1946 insight), not the ground state.

The kinetic scheme. E + S ⇌(k₁/k₋₁) ES →(k₂) EP → E + P; the steady-state treatment (Michaelis-Menten — see t6) describes how [S] fills the enzyme. The ES complex is real and observable (spectral shifts — e.g. hexokinase glucose complexes; crystal structures with trapped substrates). Catalytic perfection: when kcat/Km hits the diffusion limit (~10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ — carbonic anhydrase, acetylcholinesterase), every encounter reacts — the enzyme is as fast as physics allows.

Catalytic mechanisms (the chemistry inside). (1) Proximity/orientation: bimolecular → pseudo-unimolecular; entropy of bringing partners together is paid by binding energy (the 'effective molarity' effect — up to 10⁸-fold). (2) Strain/distortion: substrate bent toward sp²/planar transition geometry (lysozyme's boat conformation; the 'distorted sugar' model). (3) Acid–base: His (pKa ~6) shuttles protons (chymotrypsin's His⁵⁷-Asp¹⁰²-Ser¹⁹⁵ catalytic triad — Ser attacks, His deprotonates it, Asp orients/polarizes His); general acid–base at pH 7 beats water's fixed chemistry. (4) Covalent catalysis: nucleophilic attack forms a transient covalent intermediate (pyridoxal-phosphate enzymes form Schiff bases with amino acids; thiamine pyrophosphate carbanion chemistry). (5) Microenvironment: buried pockets shift pKa (an Asp in a hydrophobic site may stay protonated); desolvation strips water shells so charges interact strongly. Metal catalysis adds: Mg²⁺ positions phosphates (kinases), Zn²⁺ polarizes water (carbonic anhydrase generates OH⁻ at neutral pH), Fe/Cu cycle redox (oxidases). Binding energy (the enzyme–substrate interactions) pays for the transition-state stabilization — enzyme evolution selects tight TS binding, loose S binding.

Evidence & applications. Transition-state analogs bind 10²–10⁶× tighter than substrates (protease-inhibitor drugs — HIV protease inhibitors are TS-mimetic peptides; the design follows directly from the model). X-ray structures of ES complexes (chymotrypsin-acyl intermediates trapped). Kinetic isotope effects show which bonds break at the rate step. The model's practical face: drug design, enzyme engineering (industrial catalysts redesigned for new TS stabilization), and understanding mutations that kill catalysis while keeping binding.

g11-biology-ub3-t4.summary: The lock-and-key model captured specificity but not catalysis; induced fit (and conformational selection) shows the active site is complementary to the transition state, reshaping on binding to align catalytic groups, exclude water and strain the substrate. The cycle E+S ⇌ ES → E+P runs on a lowered activation-energy path with unchanged ΔG, powered by proximity/orientation, strain, acid–base, covalent and microenvironment/metal mechanisms. Transition-state analogs' ultra-tight binding is the model's proof — and its most profitable application.

g11-biology-ub3-t5.overview: Enzyme regulation: how cells control enzyme activity — competitive and non-competitive inhibition, allosteric control (activators, feedback inhibition), covalent modification (phosphorylation), compartmentalization, and gene-level control — the logic that keeps metabolism stable.
objectives: Distinguish competitive vs non-competitive inhibition kinetically
Explain allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition
Describe covalent regulation (phosphorylation cascades)
Give examples of medical inhibitors (statins, aspirin, methotrexate)
Summarize genetic/hormonal control of enzyme levels
g11-biology-ub3-t5.simple: A cell with 1000 enzymes running full-tilt would burn itself out — regulation is the difference between chemistry and metabolism. Inhibition: competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and fight for the active site (statins mimic HMG-CoA at reductase; methotrexate blocks folate enzymes) — out-compete them by adding more substrate (Vmax unchanged, apparent Km rises). Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and switch the enzyme down (heavy metals, cyanide on cytochrome oxidase) — Vmax falls, no substrate rescue. Allosteric control: regulatory sites distinct from the active site bind activators or inhibitors that shift the enzyme's shape (the 'on'/'off' conformations) — hemoglobin's O₂ curve is the famous cooperative S-shape; ATP inhibiting phosphofructokinase (PFK) while AMP activates it is the cell's fuel gauge. Feedback inhibition: the end product of a pathway shuts off the first committed enzyme (isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase; cholesterol inhibits HMG-CoA reductase) — the pathway throttles itself when the product is plentiful, wasting nothing. Covalent modification: phosphorylation (kinases add, phosphatases remove) flips enzyme activity — glycogen phosphorylase (on when phosphorylated — the adrenaline signal: one hormone molecule → cascade → 10⁸ glucose releases), and cascades amplify. Compartmentalization: enzymes and substrates separated by membranes (fatty-acid oxidation inside mitochondria, synthesis in cytosol — no futile cycling). Gene/hormone level: insulin induces glycolytic enzymes; lactose induces β-galactosidase; enzyme amounts are set by transcription and degradation. The big picture: instant control (allosteric, covalent, inhibitors) + slow control (gene expression) = a metabolism that responds in milliseconds and adapts in hours.
g11-biology-ub3-t5.detailed:
Inhibition kinetics. Competitive: inhibitor binds the active site (mutual exclusion with S); effect = higher [S] needed for half-maximal velocity → Km(app) increases, Vmax unchanged (surmountable); Lineweaver-Burk: lines cross on the 1/V axis. Examples: statins (mevinolin vs HMG-CoA), sulfanilamide (PABA analog in bacterial folate synthesis — selective toxicity: humans eat folate, bacteria make it — the antibiotic logic), methotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase), product inhibition (feedback's simplest form). Non-competitive: binds an allosteric site on E AND ES equally → active enzyme fraction lost → Vmax falls, Km unchanged (malonate vs succinate dehydrogenase is the classic teaching case — actually mixed; keep it simple: heavy metals, lead/mercury on –SH groups). Uncompetitive: binds only ES → both Vmax and Km fall (lithium's effects; some antibiotics).

Allostery. Conformational ensemble: T (tense, low-affinity) ↔ R (relaxed, high-affinity); ligands shift the equilibrium (Monod-Wyman-Changeux concerted model; Koshland sequential). Homotropic allostery = cooperativity (substrate itself — O₂ binding to one Hb subunit raises others' affinity → the sigmoid curve; physiological payoff: load O₂ in lungs, unload in tissues — Bohr effect: CO₂/H⁺ shift the curve right where needed). Heterotropic: regulators at separate sites — ATP inhibits PFK (energy-rich → slow glycolysis), AMP/ADP activate (energy-hungry → accelerate); CTP inhibits aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase — the classic; the pyrimidine end product throttles its own pathway's first step); the regulatory and catalytic subunits separate (ATCase's c₆r₃ architecture).

Feedback & feed-forward. End-product inhibition of the first committed step (isoleucine from threonine; the pathway's flux matches demand; prevents intermediate pile-up). Sequential feedback (each branch of a branched pathway inhibited by its own product; concerted feedback when all products required). Feed-forward activation: early substrate accelerates later steps (glycolytic flux coupling). The engineering view: negative feedback = stability + demand-matching; the cell invented control theory.

Covalent & proteolytic control. Phosphorylation: ~100+ kinases, few hundred phosphatases; Ser/Thr/Tyr modification changes charge/shape → switches activity (glycogen phosphorylase activated by phosphorylation cascade: adrenaline → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase — 10⁸-fold amplification; glycogen synthase the reverse — reciprocal control prevents futile cycles). Other modifications: adenylylation (glutamine synthetase), Ca²⁺/calmodulin (kinases), redox switches, limited proteolysis (zymogens — irreversible activation: digestion, clotting, apoptosis cascades).

Levels of control. Compartmentalization (mitochondrial β-oxidation vs cytosolic lipogenesis; lysosomal hydrolases at pH 5). Enzyme amount: transcriptional induction/repression (lac operon — lactose/allolactose inactivates the repressor; catabolite repression — glucose preference), hormonal enzyme synthesis (insulin induces glucokinase; starvation enzymes degrade), degradation (ubiquitin-proteasome — tagged proteins recycled). Isozymes: tissue-specific variants with different kinetics (hexokinase low-Km everywhere vs glucokinase high-Km liver — the liver only buffers glucose when blood levels are high; LDH isoforms — heart vs muscle patterns). The integrated answer: metabolism is regulated at every timescale — milliseconds (allosteric), seconds (covalent), minutes-hours (gene expression).

workedExamples.substitution: sulfanilamide competes with PABA at dihydropteroate synthase (folate synthesis); bacteria must MAKE folate (blocked → death); humans EAT folate (no pathway to block → safe)
workedExamples.answer: The first antibiotic worked because the target enzyme exists in the pathogen and not in us

Thinking feedback inhibition is permanent — it's rapid and reversible (product falls → enzyme reactivates)
Believing phosphorylation always activates — it switches (glycogen SYNTHASE is inactivated by phosphorylation)

Aspirin: irreversibly acetylates COX (prostaglandin synthesis) — covalent inhibition as analgesic

Cyanide poisoning: cytochrome-c-oxidase block — non-competitive lethality; thiosulfate therapy
Diabetes drugs: sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels; metformin activates AMPK — the energy gauge as pharmacy
g11-biology-ub3-t5.summary: Cells regulate enzymes at every timescale: reversible inhibitors (competitive — active-site contest, surmountable; non-competitive — Vmax loss), allosteric switches (T/R conformations; ATP/AMP energy gauges; cooperativity), feedback inhibition of committed steps (end products throttle their own pathways), covalent modification (phosphorylation cascades with huge amplification; zymogen proteolysis for one-way activation), compartmentalization, and gene-level control of enzyme amounts (operons, hormones, isozymes). Metabolism is chemistry under control — and its control logic is medicine's favorite target.

g11-biology-ub3-t6.overview: Factors affecting enzyme action: substrate concentration (Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Km, Vmax), enzyme concentration, temperature (Q₁₀ and the optimum curve), pH (ionization and denaturation), and inhibitor/cofactor availability — the quantitative environment of catalysis.
objectives: Interpret the Michaelis-Menten curve and define Vmax and Km
Explain enzyme concentration effects
Describe the temperature–activity curve and optimum
Explain pH optima and ionization effects
Relate cofactors/inhibitors to activity in real systems
g11-biology-ub3-t6.simple: Enzyme activity depends on its environment. Substrate concentration: at low [S], rate rises almost linearly (plenty of free enzyme); as [S] climbs, active sites saturate and the curve bends to a ceiling — Vmax (all enzyme busy — adding substrate can't help). The Michaelis constant Km is the [S] giving half-Vmax: a LOW Km means high affinity (the enzyme grabs substrate at tiny concentrations — hexokinase Km ~0.1 mM; glucokinase's high Km ~10 mM suits the liver's glucose-buffering job). Enzyme concentration: with substrate saturating, rate is directly proportional to [E] — double the enzyme, double the rate (this is why measuring 'how much enzyme' works in diagnostics — ALT/AST blood levels flag liver damage). Temperature: two opposing effects — warming speeds molecular motion (~2× per 10 °C, the Q₁₀ rule) but also denatures the protein; the net is a bell curve peaking at the optimum (human enzymes ~37 °C; thermophilus bacteria from hot springs — Taq polymerase's 72 °C optimum made PCR possible). pH: each enzyme has an optimum (pepsin 2, trypsin 8, most cytosolic ~7.2) because active-site residues must be in the right ionization state to catalyze, and extreme pH also denatures. Cofactors: no Mg²⁺, no kinase activity; no NAD⁺, no dehydrogenase. Inhibitors: competitive/non-competitive (see t5). The quantitative frame: Michaelis-Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]); the double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot straightens it — and Km/Vmax are the enzyme's fingerprint, measured the same way in every lab on Earth.
g11-biology-ub3-t6.detailed:
Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Assumptions: initial velocity (before product accumulates), steady state (d[ES]/dt ≈ 0 — formation = breakdown), [S] ≫ [E]. Derivation: E+S ⇌ ES → E+P; with k₂ ≫ k₋₁ sometimes (Briggs-Haldane general). v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]); Km = (k₋₁+k₂)/k₁ — the dissociation-like constant; when [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2; Vmax = kcat[E]ₜ. Low [S]: v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S] — first-order, the specificity constant Vmax/Km governs. High [S]: v → Vmax — zero-order (enzyme saturated — the basis of dosing: alcohol dehydrogenase's Km for ethanol is ~1 mM but blood ethanol reaches 100+ mM → elimination is constant-rate (~0.1 g/dL/h) — why you can't 'speed up' sobriety). kcat/Km > 10⁸ = diffusion-limited perfection. Lineweaver-Burk: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax — intercepts give both constants; inhibition patterns cross differently (competitive: same 1/Vmax, different slope).

Enzyme concentration. v ∝ [E] at saturating [S] — the linear assay principle; in cells, [E] is set by synthesis/degradation (see t5 gene control). Diagnostic enzymes: normally compartmentalized, appear in blood when tissue damages — CK-MB (heart), ALT/AST (liver), amylase (pancreas), LDH isozymes — activity measured by M-M kinetics.

Temperature. Rate rises with kinetic energy (Arrhenius; Q₁₀ ≈ 2 for most biological rates) until thermal agitation breaks the weak bonds of tertiary structure → denaturation (irreversible for most; the cooking-egg asymmetry). Optimum = the balance point; human enzymes ~37 °C (fever above 42 °C denatures — the danger ceiling), thermophiles 70–100 °C (Taq: 72 °C optimum — more salt bridges, compact hydrophobic cores, chaperonines), psychrophiles (Antarctic fish: flexible active sites work near 0 °C — the flexibility/stability trade-off). Cold: slows but usually preserves (why enzymes are stored at −20 °C; hibernation's metabolic throttle).

pH. Catalytic residues (His, Asp, Glu, Cys, Lys) must hold specific protonation states for acid–base/covalent chemistry; the bell-shaped pH–activity curve reflects two pKa transitions (too acidic/too basic each kills a required state). Extreme pH also denatures (charge repulsion unfolds). Optima track compartments: pepsin 1.5–2 (stomach), trypsin 7.5–8.5 (duodenum), acid phosphatase ~5 (lysosome), alkaline phosphatase ~10 (bone/intestine membrane). Buffers in blood/cytoplasm keep pH within survival bands (7.35–7.45 — outside 6.8/7.8 = death — enzyme failure is why).

Cofactors, inhibitors, water activity. Metal/coenzyme dependence: apo vs holo (EDTA chelation kills metalloenzymes; vitamin deficiency = coenzyme starvation). Reversible inhibitors (t5) shift the curves; irreversible inhibitors (aspirin-acetylated COX, organophosphates on acetylcholinesterase) remove enzyme permanently — recovery needs new synthesis. Water activity: dry enzymes are inert (why honey and salt preserve — microbes' enzymes lose their solvent); osmotic stress concentrates/restricts. Substrate inhibition: very high [S] sometimes slows (second substrate molecule binds a non-productive site). The full picture: activity = f([E], [S], T, pH, cofactors, inhibitors, water) — and the cell controls every term.

Clinical labs: enzyme activity assays at saturating [S] quantify biomarkers (CK, ALT, lipase)
Agriculture: herbicide design targets plant-specific enzyme kinetics (glyphosate's EPSP affinity)
g11-biology-ub3-t6.summary: Enzyme activity is a function of its conditions: substrate concentration follows Michaelis-Menten saturation (Vmax = kcat[E]ₜ; Km = half-saturation, low Km = high affinity); enzyme concentration scales rate linearly when saturated; temperature gives a bell curve (Q₁₀ acceleration vs denaturation — the 37 °C optimum, Taq's 72 °C); pH curves reflect active-site ionization (pepsin 2, trypsin 8); cofactors and inhibitors complete the control set. These constants are the quantitative language of biochemistry — and of medicine.

g11-biology-ub3-t7.overview: Industrial applications of enzymes: immobilization, detergent and food processing, brewing and fermentation, textile and paper treatment, diagnostics and medicine, and the biotechnology of extremozymes — biology's catalysts as industry's tools.
objectives: Explain enzyme immobilization and its industrial advantages
Describe detergent, food, and brewing enzyme applications
Summarize textile, paper and leather enzyme uses
Give diagnostic and therapeutic enzyme products
Evaluate extremozymes and industrial biotechnology
g11-biology-ub3-t7.simple: Industry rents enzymes because they work fast, specific and clean — at 30–60 °C, in water, without heavy metals, leaving no toxic residue. The trick that makes them economical: immobilization — trapping enzyme beads on/in a support (alginate gel, resin, cloth) so they're reused for months instead of washed away; immobilized enzymes give continuous production (substrate flows in, product flows out), easy separation (no enzyme in the food), and stability. Products everywhere: detergents (protease + amylase + lipase + cellulase — biological powders that digest blood, starch, fat and smooth cotton at 30 °C — the energy saving of cold washing), food (high-fructose corn syrup: amylase + glucose isomerase converting corn starch to sweeter fructose — the biggest enzyme process on Earth; lactase for lactose-free milk; rennet chymosin for cheese — now recombinant; pectinase for clear juices; papain for meat tenderizing), brewing (barley malt amylases converting grain starch to fermentable sugars — the same Buchner chemistry behind injera's fermentation), textiles (cellulase 'stone-washing' denim — enzymes replaced pumice stones; amylase desizing; catalase after peroxide bleaching), paper (xylanases bleach without chlorine — the dioxin problem solved), leather (protease dehairing replaces lime — less toxic tanneries), medicine/diagnostics (glucose oxidase test strips — the diabetic meter's enzyme; PCR's Taq polymerase; clot-busting streptokinase/tPA; digestive enzyme supplements; papain debridement), and biotechnology (restriction enzymes + ligase = genetic engineering; cellulases converting crop waste to bioethanol — the second-generation fuel). Extremozymes: enzymes from hot-spring and salt-lake organisms (Taq at 72 °C; alkaline proteases at pH 10; psychrophilic lipases in cold washes) — evolution pre-engineered the industrial specs. The economics: enzymes cut energy, water, chemicals and waste — green chemistry's first success story.
g11-biology-ub3-t7.detailed:
Immobilization technology. Methods: adsorption (weak-physisorption to resins — easy, leaches), entrapment (alginate/polyacrylamide gel beads — the school-lab classic with yeast; no leakage, diffusion-limited), covalent binding (glutaraldehyde to supports — stable, may distort the site), cross-linking (glutaraldehyde between enzyme molecules — carrier-free). Advantages: reuse (cost per unit product collapses), continuous packed-bed reactors (glucose isomerase columns produce millions of tonnes of HFCS/year), product purity (no enzyme contamination — critical in food), stability gains (rigidified conformation resists denaturation), instant reaction stop (remove the beads). Costs: mass-transfer limitation (substrate must diffuse into the bead — the 'diffusion barrier' lowers apparent rate), support expense, activity loss over cycles. Whole-cell immobilization (yeast, bacteria) is cheaper when the enzyme needs cofactors regenerated inside the cell.

Food & fermentation. HFCS: corn starch →(α-amylase, liquefaction 90 °C, Ca²⁺) dextrins →(glucoamylase) glucose →(glucose isomerase, immobilized, 60 °C) fructose syrup (42–55% fructose — sweeter than sucrose, cheap from US corn — the public-health controversy is economic, not enzymatic). Cheese: chymosin (rennet) cleaves κ-casein → micelles coagulate; recombinant chymosin (from cloned gene in E. coli/Aspergillus — the first FDA-approved GM enzyme, 1990) ended calf-stomach dependence. Juice: pectinase (polygalacturonase) clears cloudiness + boosts yield. Lactose-free milk: immobilized lactase hydrolyzes lactose → glucose + galactose. Baking: amylase (improves loaf volume), oxidase (strengthens dough). Brewing: malt enzymes (α/β-amylase, limit dextrinase, proteases) during mashing define wort fermentability — the traditional process is applied enzymology; Ethiopia's tej and injera fermentations run on grain + microbial enzymes (Buchner's zymase lineage).

Detergents & textiles. Laundry enzymes: alkaline proteases (Subtilisin — Bacillus licheniformis; works pH 9–11, digests protein stains: blood, egg), amylases (starch), lipases (fats — now engineered to attack triglycerides without bile), cellulases (fabric care — remove fibrils, keep colors bright). Formulation constraints: must survive bleach (peroxide), surfactants and drying — protein engineering created bleach-resistant variants (Novo's history — the enzyme-detergent industry began with a 1913 Bacillus extract patent). Cold washing: enzymes' mild-condition catalysis saves the ~60% of a washer's energy spent heating water. Textiles: desizing (amylase removes starch sizing), bio-polishing (cellulase smooths cotton), stone-washing (cellulase replaces pumice — uniform fades, less machine wear), denim bleaching with laccase (replaces permanganate — the 'whisker' look without the worker-harm chemical).

Paper, leather, feed, biofuels. Pulp bleaching: xylanases reduce chlorine dioxide use (dioxin risk ↓); pitch control (lipases); deinking (cellulases/endoglucanases in recycling). Leather: protease-lipase dehairing replaces sodium sulfide/lime (the Bati tannery pollution story — enzymes cut the effluent load); bating (protease softening). Feed: phytase (the revolution — releases phosphorus from grain phytate, cutting phosphate pollution and mined-P use; monogastric animals lack native phytase), NSP enzymes (arabinoxylanases improve poultry growth). Biofuels: cellulosic ethanol needs cellulase cocktails (Trichoderma; engineered for cost — the enzyme price was the bottleneck; consolidated bioprocessing with engineered microbes). Molasses/ethanol fermentation: yeast zymase — the same pathway Buchner demonstrated.

Medicine & diagnostics. Diagnostic strips: glucose oxidase/dehydrogenase + electrode — the glucometer (immobilized-enzyme biosensor — Clark's oxygen electrode lineage); lactate, urea, cholesterol strips. Therapeutics: streptokinase/tPA (fibrinolysis — clot busting), hyaluronidase (spreading agent), asparaginase (leukemia — tumor cells can't make the amino acid), lipase/protease/amylase supplements (pancreatic insufficiency — the enzyme-replacement logic), papain (wound debridement). Research: restriction endonucleases + DNA ligase + polymerases = recombinant DNA technology (the enzyme toolkit that built biotech); Taq polymerase → PCR (Nobel 1993; the hot-spring enzyme that made molecular biology routine — and made Ethiopian genotyping labs possible). The pattern: every industry that touches molecules touches enzymes — and the design rule is matching enzyme specs (pH, T, specificity, cofactor) to process conditions, or engineering the enzyme to fit.

workedExamples.problem: A juice plant switches from filtration alone to pectinase treatment. Predict three changes.
workedExamples.substitution: pectin (the cloud-stabilizer + gel network) hydrolyzed → clarity ↑, viscosity ↓ → filtration rate ↑ (2–5×), yield ↑ (juice trapped in pectin released); cost: enzyme + hold time, but less energy/chemical
workedExamples.answer: Enzyme replaced mechanical work — clearer juice, faster line, higher recovery

workedExamples.problem: Why is immobilized glucose isomerase run in packed beds at 60 °C rather than mixed into syrup tanks?
workedExamples.substitution: the enzyme is expensive and the substrate is cheap → continuous column = months of reuse; 60 °C raises rate (Q₁₀) and fructose's sweetness equilibrium; no enzyme leaches into the product (food safety); diffusion limitation managed by bead size
workedExamples.answer: Immobilization turns a one-shot reagent into a permanent factory part

workedExamples.problem: Poultry feed lacks native phytase; grain locks 60–70% of its phosphorus. Explain the enzyme's double payoff.
workedExamples.substitution: microbial phytase in the gut hydrolyzes phytate → P + myo-inositol absorbed → less mined-dicalcium-phosphate added (cost ↓) AND less P excreted (water eutrophication ↓); one enzyme, two savings
workedExamples.answer: Phytase converts an anti-nutrient into nutrition while cutting pollution

workedExamples.problem: PCR failed until Taq polymerase arrived. Connect the enzyme's property to the technique's need.
workedExamples.substitution: PCR cycles to 95 °C (denature) each round; mesophilic polymerases died every cycle (manual re-adding — the old laborious way); Taq (Thermus aquaticus, hot springs) survives 95 °C and works at 72 °C → automation, exponential amplification from one tube
workedExamples.answer: A hot-spring enzyme's stability made molecular biology scalable

workedExamples.problem: A detergent claims 'removes blood stains at 30 °C.' Name the enzyme and the mechanism.
workedExamples.substitution: alkaline protease (subtilisin) hydrolyzes hemoglobin/serum proteins into soluble peptides → stain lifts; 30 °C works because enzymes don't need heat — the energy saving vs 60 °C washes is the point
workedExamples.calculation: Q₁₀ at mild T still fast enough
workedExamples.answer: Biological detergents trade hot water for catalysis — cleaner clothes, lower bills

commonMistakes: 'Immobilization always improves enzymes' — it adds diffusion limits and can lower activity; it's bought for reuse and separation
Confusing rennet with rennin (renin) — chymosin is the cheese enzyme, not the kidney hormone
Thinking enzyme detergents are 'stronger chemicals' — they're catalysts; they digest stains, not fabric
Believing HFCS is 'an enzyme product that's dangerous' — the enzyme is benign; the metabolic debate is about dose and sugar chemistry
Calling PCR 'just heating and cooling' — its feasibility was a protein-stability problem (Taq solved it)
Assuming industrial enzymes come from factories — most are microbial (Bacillus, Aspergillus, Trichoderma) fermented
Thinking enzyme processes are 'new age' — brewing and cheese are 6000-year-old enzymology
applications: HFCS & biofuels: the two giant enzyme processes — sugar and fuel from starch by catalysis
Glucometers: glucose oxidase strips — immobilized-enzyme diagnostics in millions of homes
Ethiopian brewing/injera: traditional amylase/zymase fermentations — indigenous enzymology
Leather dehairing: enzyme processes cutting tannery toxicity — industrial ecology
Recombinant chymosin & insulin: the GM-enzyme era — cloned genes, fermented proteins
g11-biology-ub3-t7.summary: Industry uses enzymes as reusable, specific, mild-condition catalysts: immobilization (entrapment, binding, packed beds) makes them economical; the flagship processes are HFCS (glucose isomerase), detergents (alkaline proteases), cheese (recombinant chymosin), juice (pectinase), feed (phytase), paper (xylanase), diagnostics (glucose oxidase strips) and PCR (Taq). Extremozymes supply the robustness; green chemistry supplies the rationale — less energy, water, chlorine and waste. From ancient injera fermentation to engineered biocatalysts, enzymes are biology's industrial gift.
